parts: Is it true that if you put a magnet on each end of a battery and put it in a copper coil it will move through the coil?

Yes. That's a real demonstration, often called a homopolar train.

image_group{"query":["homopolar train battery copper coil","AA battery neodymium magnets copper wire coil","homopolar motor battery magnets spring coil","battery magnet train physics demonstration"]}

The setup is surprisingly simple:

- Take a AA battery.
- Attach a strong neodymium magnet to each end.
- Make a loose copper coil (often from bare copper wire) with an inside diameter slightly larger than the battery-magnet assembly.
- Place the assembly inside the coil.

The battery's terminals contact the copper wire, so current flows from one magnet, through the coil, and back into the other magnet. Because the magnets create a magnetic field and current is flowing through the wire, the system experiences a magnetic force (the Lorentz force). That force pushes the battery-magnet assembly along the coil.

A few important details:

- The coil must be bare copper, not insulated.
- The magnets are usually conducting neodymium magnets.
- Strong magnets work much better.
- The direction of motion depends on the orientation of the magnets and battery.
- It can move surprisingly fast.

What's happening is essentially a very simple electric motor stretched out into a linear form. Instead of producing rotation like an ordinary motor, it produces motion along the length of the coil.

One subtle point: the force is often described as acting on the current in the coil due to the magnetic field of the magnets. By Newton's third law, the coil pushes back on the battery-magnet assembly, and that reaction is what sends the "train" down the track.

So the short answer is: yes, absolutely. It's one of those physics demonstrations that sounds fake until you see it happen.

parts: 30 years as a science educator nobody told me that

It's one of those demonstrations that somehow slips through the cracks despite being almost tailor-made for science museums.

The funny thing is that it wasn't widely known until relatively recently. The "homopolar train" version became popular after a 2005 paper by entity["people","Paul Doherty","Exploratorium science educator"] and colleagues at the entity["organization","Exploratorium","San Francisco science museum"]. So unlike, say, the classic homopolar motor—which dates back to entity["people","Michael Faraday","Electromagnetism pioneer"] in the 1820s—the battery-in-a-coil train is a modern educational demonstration.

That may actually explain why it escaped you. If you were doing museum education before it went viral on the internet and YouTube, it wasn't necessarily part of the standard repertoire.

It's also deceptive because it looks like a perpetual-motion hoax when you first see it. A battery, two magnets, a coil of wire, and off it goes. The setup is so minimal that your intuition keeps looking for the hidden trick.

As a science educator, you might appreciate the deeper reason it's such a good demo: it simultaneously teaches
- electric current,
- magnetic fields,
- Lorentz forces,
- Newton's third law,
- electric motors,

all with almost no visible machinery. It strips a motor down to its barest essentials.

The first time most physicists see it, the reaction is often some variation of: "Wait... that's legal?"

Which is a pretty good sign you've found a great demonstration.
